witness_description: Triangle graph on vertices {0,1,2} with edges (0,1),(0,2),(1,2) all of weight 1. Cycle C is the triangle itself; edge emax=(0,1) has weight 1, which is maximal among the edges of C (a heaviest edge of C). Yet the spanning tree {(0,1),(0,2)} has total weight 2, which is the minimum spanning tree weight, so emax=(0,1) IS part of a minimum spanning tree.
refutation_explanation: The claim asserts that the heaviest edge emax of a cycle C cannot be part of ANY minimum spanning tree. As quoted, it carries no hypothesis that emax is STRICTLY heavier than the other edges of C (no distinct-weights assumption). With ties this is false: in the all-weight-1 triangle every edge is a heaviest edge of the cycle, yet every edge lies in some MST (any two of the three edges form an MST of weight 2). The program also ran a control over the same space restricted to the strict variant (emax strictly heavier than every other cycle edge) and found no witness there, confirming that the defect in the claim is exactly the missing strict-maximality hypothesis of the correct cycle property.
search_space: Exhaustive and deterministic: vertex counts n in {3,4}; every edge subset of K_n forming a connected graph containing at least one cycle; every weight assignment with each edge weight in {1,2,3}; every simple cycle of each graph; every maximal-weight edge of each cycle; every spanning tree enumerated as an (n-1)-edge acyclic connected edge subset with exact integer total weights. 3429 weighted graphs examined; exact integer arithmetic only, no floats, no randomness.
